title: Integrity Is a Control System, Not a Character Trait
summary: Integrity in development is not a feeling about yourself; it is a set of checks that prove where money came from, who really owns it, and that nothing of value is passing to an official or a sanctioned party. Learn the four controls and you can raise money, bank and sell without a hidden defect in the deal.
body:
Mr Shabazz, an honest developer can still take dirty money, pay a bribe through an agent or sell to a sanctioned buyer without meaning to. Integrity, in practice, is four controls that make those things hard to do by accident: know who you deal with, know where their money came from, never pay for a public decision, and never deal with a listed party.

Recall

Q. What is misrepresentation in an offering document?

A. A statement of fact that is untrue, or an omission of a fact needed to make what was said not misleading, that a reasonable investor would treat as important. It can expose the issuer and the people who signed the document to claims for loss.

Q. What makes an arrangement a security, in concept?

A. Broadly, an investment of money in a common enterprise where the investor expects a return from the efforts of others. The exact test is jurisdictional; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. In an exit, what is the core difference between an asset sale and a share sale?

A. In an asset sale the buyer takes the building and the seller's company keeps its history; in a share sale the buyer takes the company, including its tax attributes and its liabilities. Tax and liability fall differently in each.

Why this matters

A development company handles large sums from people it does not know well: investors, buyers, lenders, joint venture partners, landowners. It also needs decisions from people with public power: planners, inspectors, utility officials, customs officers. Those two facts make real estate one of the sectors regulators watch most closely for money laundering and corruption. Property is a good place to hide value: large, durable, easy to resell, often bought through companies.

The cost of a failure here is not a fine alone. A bank closes your accounts. An investor's money is frozen in your project account. A buyer cannot get title insurance. A future lender's compliance team reads the newspaper archive and declines. You can lose access to the financial system faster than you can lose a building. That is why I treat integrity as a control system, with procedures, records and an owner, rather than as a quality you either have or lack.

Control one: know your counterparty

In plain English: before you take money from someone, or pay money to someone, find out who they really are.

The professional framing is know your customer, abbreviated KYC: the process of identifying a counterparty and verifying that identity with reliable documents. For a person, that means a government identity document and proof of address. For a company, it means its registration documents, its directors and, most importantly, its beneficial owners. A beneficial owner is the natural person who ultimately owns or controls the entity, however many companies sit in between. Many regimes set a threshold for which owners must be identified, often a significant share such as a quarter of the votes or value, plus anyone who controls the entity by other means; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

A worked example, hypothetical. An investor offers 1,000,000 dollars of equity through Company A. Company A is owned 60 percent by Company B and 40 percent by a named individual. Company B is owned equally by two people. Multiply down the chain: each of the two owners of Company B holds 50 percent of 60 percent, which is 30 percent of Company A. The named individual holds 40 percent. All three exceed a 25 percent test, so all three are beneficial owners you identify and verify. If any one of them refuses, you do not have an investor. You have a question.

Control two: know where the money came from

In plain English: knowing who someone is does not tell you where their money came from.

Two terms are easy to confuse. Source of funds is the origin of the specific money in this transaction: this wire came from the sale of that property, through this account. Source of wealth is how the person built their overall wealth: a business, an inheritance, a career. You test source of funds with documents that trace the money, and you test source of wealth for plausibility against the size of the commitment.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A buyer of a 600,000 dollar condominium unit says the deposit comes from the sale of a house. The sale statement shows a price of 900,000 dollars, a mortgage payout of 400,000 dollars and fees of 40,000 dollars, leaving 460,000 dollars. A 120,000 dollar deposit fits comfortably inside that. If the buyer then wires the deposit from a third party's account in another country, the story and the money no longer match. That mismatch, not the country, is the red flag. You ask before you accept, and you record what you asked and what you were told.

Say that out loud now.

I identify every beneficial owner, I trace the money, and when the story and the money do not match, I stop and ask.

Controls three and four: bribery and sanctions

Bribery is offering or giving anything of value to improperly influence a decision. Value includes cash, gifts, travel, jobs for relatives, donations and inflated consulting fees. Most modern anti-bribery laws reach payments made through agents and intermediaries, and several hold companies liable for failing to prevent bribery by people acting for them. Some regimes once allowed small facilitation payments to speed routine actions; several have narrowed or removed that exception [unverified — confirm independently]. Treat every facilitation payment as forbidden unless your lawyer tells you otherwise in writing.

Sanctions are legal prohibitions on dealing with named people, entities or countries. They are close to strict: an intention to do right does not excuse a deal with a listed party. Screening means checking every counterparty, and its beneficial owners, against the relevant lists before you sign and again before you pay.

How the best do it

Large contractors and institutional owners run what they call third-party due diligence: every agent, consultant and joint venture partner is risk-rated before engagement, high-risk ones get enhanced checks, contracts carry anti-corruption representations and audit rights, and payments go only to accounts in the counterparty's own name in the country where the work is done. A small developer can copy the core of it with a one-page intake form, a screening search, a written approval for anyone rated high risk, and a rule that no payment goes to a third party's account.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: unexplained cash and round-tripped funds attract tax enquiries as well as AML ones; documented source of funds protects both. Liability: directors can be personally exposed for corporate bribery or sanctions breaches in many regimes; verify against the primary source. Banking: your bank runs KYC on you; a clean investor file keeps your accounts open. Governance: name one person accountable for the integrity file and require board approval for high-risk counterparties. Estate: heirs inherit assets and the reputational and legal history attached to them. Exit: a buyer's diligence will ask for your KYC records; missing ones cut the price or kill the sale.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the trusted introducer: a respected person vouches for an investor or an agent, and the checks are skipped because asking feels rude. The control is a rule with no exceptions: everyone goes through the same file, and the introducer's reputation is recorded, not relied on.

The beginner's mistake

Treating KYC as the bank's job. The bank checks you. It does not check your investors, your agents or your buyers on your behalf, and in many regimes developers have their own reporting duties [unverified — confirm independently].

Callback

In Week 24, Elias and Cole drew the line between avoidance and evasion: substance over form. The same test runs here. A layered ownership chain is legal form; the beneficial owner is the substance. A consulting fee is form; what the consultant actually does is the substance. Integrity checks are substance checks.

Recap

Four controls: know your counterparty and its beneficial owners, trace the source of funds and test the source of wealth, never pay for a public decision directly or through anyone, and screen every party against sanctions lists before signing and paying.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: Odebrecht and the bribery department that ran like a business unit.
checklist: I identify and verify every beneficial owner above the threshold, and anyone with control by other means.
I trace the source of funds for every investor and buyer deposit.
I test source of wealth for plausibility against the size of the commitment.
I screen every counterparty and its owners against sanctions lists before signing and before paying.
I pay only into accounts in the counterparty's own name.
I treat facilitation payments as forbidden unless counsel says otherwise in writing.
I keep a written integrity file with one named owner.
head: Field checklist
speak: Integrity in a development company is a control system, not a character trait. It has four controls. First, know your counterparty: identify every investor, buyer, agent and partner, and find the beneficial owners, the real people behind any chain of companies. Multiply down the chain to see who crosses the threshold. Second, know where the money came from. Source of funds is the trail for this specific money; source of wealth is how the person became able to invest at all. When the story and the money do not match, I stop and ask, and I write down the answer. Third, never pay anything of value for a public decision, directly or through an agent, and treat facilitation payments as forbidden. Fourth, screen every party against sanctions lists before I sign and again before I pay. The biggest risk is the trusted introducer whose word replaces the file. Everyone goes through the same file.
terms: Know your customer (KYC) — the process of identifying a counterparty and verifying that identity with reliable documents before dealing with it.
Beneficial owner — the natural person who ultimately owns or controls an entity, however many companies sit in between.
Source of funds — the documented origin of the specific money used in a transaction, as distinct from source of wealth, which is how the person built their overall wealth.

hostile.q: Your largest investor holds through three offshore companies. Who is the beneficial owner, and how do you know?
hostile.a: I can name them, and I can show you how. I have the register of each company in the chain, the share percentages multiplied down to each natural person, verified identity documents for everyone above the threshold, a sanctions and adverse-media screen dated this month, and a source-of-funds trail for the wire into our account. If any piece is missing, the money is not drawn until it is complete.

title: Odebrecht: When Bribery Became a Department
summary: The Brazilian construction group Odebrecht ran a dedicated unit to pay bribes for public contracts across several countries, until Brazil's Operation Car Wash and a 2016 global plea agreement exposed it. Seven forensic steps show how a normal-looking business decision became an institution. Cole joins on the legal side.
body:
Odebrecht did not drift into corruption one envelope at a time. It built a business unit for it, with staff, systems and offshore accounts, because winning public contracts that way looked cheaper than competing for them. The lesson for a small developer is about how ordinary the first step feels.

Recall

Q. What are the two parts of source-of-funds and source-of-wealth checks?

A. Source of funds traces the specific money in this transaction; source of wealth tests whether the person's overall wealth plausibly supports the commitment.

Q. What duty of reporting does a sponsor owe investors after closing, in concept?

A. To report accurately and on time what the offering documents promised: financial results, material events and conflicts. The exact duties depend on the documents and the governing law.

Q. What is a departure tax, in concept?

A. A tax charge some systems apply when a person stops being resident, treating assets as if sold at market value on the day of departure. Rules differ widely; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole sits with me today because the most useful parts of this case are legal: what the company admitted, and how liability reached far beyond the people who carried the money. I have kept to facts that are on the public record and well established. Where I describe the company's internal habits, I describe them in general terms, as the plea documents and wide reporting do. Before you cite any detail in a meeting, confirm it against the primary sources.

1. Timeline

Odebrecht was one of Latin America's largest engineering and construction groups, building roads, dams, ports, stadiums and energy plants. In March 2014 Brazilian federal investigators opened what became known as Operation Car Wash, or Lava Jato, which began as a money-laundering inquiry and widened into bribery around contracts with the state oil company Petrobras. In June 2015 the group's chief executive, Marcelo Odebrecht, was arrested. In December 2016 Odebrecht and its petrochemical affiliate Braskem entered a coordinated resolution with authorities in the United States, Brazil and Switzerland, including guilty pleas in a United States federal court. The admissions described a dedicated division that managed bribe payments across many countries. Political fallout spread across the region for years, and in 2019 the group entered court-supervised reorganisation in Brazil.

2. Key decisions

The decisive choice was to institutionalise the payments: to give them a budget, a staff and a parallel accounting system kept apart from the ordinary books. Once a function has a budget, it has targets, and once it has targets, it grows. The second decision was to pay through offshore companies and intermediaries so that no payment looked like what it was. The third was to keep doing it after the investigation was public.

3. Assumptions

The assumptions were the kind that sound like realism. That everyone in the market paid, so refusing meant losing. That officials would protect the company because they were implicated too. That layered offshore payments could not be traced. That a company of national importance was too large to be prosecuted. Each assumption failed. Investigators followed the money through banks in several countries, cooperating witnesses described the system, and size turned out to multiply the exposure rather than shield it.

4. Incentives

Executives were rewarded for winning contracts, and a bribe bought a contract more reliably than a better bid. Officials were rewarded personally for steering awards. Intermediaries earned fees for moving money. Nobody inside the loop was paid to say no. Cole's point here matters: incentives explain behaviour, but they do not excuse it in law. Anti-bribery statutes in many jurisdictions make the company liable for what its people and agents do on its behalf.

Say that out loud now.

If nobody is paid to say no, I must be the one who is.

5. Warning signs ignored

Payments to consultants whose work nobody could describe. Fees routed to accounts in countries where no work was performed. Contract awards that arrived suspiciously fast or on terms competitors could not match. Cash moving through a separate system outside the audited books. And, after 2014, a public investigation naming the company's counterparties. Every one of these is a standard red flag in an anti-corruption manual.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the moment the payments became a department. Before that, individual corrupt acts could be stopped, reported and disciplined. After it, the company's revenue depended on the system, so shutting it down meant losing contracts, and the people who knew about it had every reason to keep it running. A system is far harder to stop than a lapse.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a decision to treat public decisions as something you can buy, then to build a cost centre around buying them. The control that would have stopped it is simple to state and hard to keep: no payment to any intermediary without visible work, a defensible price and an account in the intermediary's own name, checked before engagement and audited after.

Cole's view: how liability travelled

Three legal mechanics are worth your attention, in concept. First, corporate liability: the company was liable for acts of employees and agents done for its benefit. Second, books and records: some statutes treat false accounting of a payment as an offence on its own, separate from the bribe. Third, reach: one country's anti-bribery law can apply to conduct elsewhere when its currency, banks or markets are used. The specifics vary; verify against the primary source before you rely on any of them.

When the market seems to expect it

The hardest version of this lesson is the one where you believe you will lose the deal by refusing. Here is the practical sequence. Refuse plainly and without accusation: we do not make payments of that kind. Write down what was asked, by whom and when, the same day. Tell your lawyer and, where the request came from inside an authority, ask whether there is a formal complaint route. Then use the legitimate tools that remain: the published timeline for the approval, a written request for the status of the file, an escalation to the official's supervisor, and an appeal where the law gives one.

Sometimes you will lose time this way, and occasionally you will lose a deal. Price that honestly. A delayed approval costs carrying cost for some months. A paid bribe costs the approval itself, which can be voided, plus the exposure of every person who signed for it, plus your bank. One is a schedule risk. The other is an existential one.

The biggest risk

For a small developer the risk is not a department. It is one agent, retained to get a permit moving, whose fee is larger than the work and whose account is somewhere else. The control is Rule 72, applied to the first agent, not the fiftieth.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that a payment through a third party is the third party's problem. Most modern anti-bribery regimes are written precisely so that it is yours. The second mistake is thinking a small payment is a small risk. The exposure is set by what the payment was for, not by its size.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught how to instruct and challenge professionals. The same discipline applies to agents and consultants: a written scope, a deliverable you can see and a fee you can explain. An agent you cannot instruct in writing is an agent you should not retain.

Recap

Odebrecht turned bribery from an act into a system, routed it through intermediaries and offshore accounts, and was exposed by investigators who followed the money. Liability reached the company through its agents and its books.

Rule 72: Never let anyone pay for a public decision on your behalf; every agent, consultant and intermediary must show work you can see, be paid into their own account at a price you can defend, and be checked before engagement, not after.

Next: Roman on The Money: what integrity costs, and what a single tainted investor does to your returns.
checklist: I give every agent and consultant a written scope and a deliverable I can inspect.
I compare every intermediary's fee with the market price for the work.
I pay intermediaries only into accounts in their own name, in the country where they work.
I run due diligence on every intermediary before engagement.
I keep every payment inside the audited books, with no side ledgers.
I escalate any request for an unexplained or urgent payment to counsel.
I re-check intermediaries whenever a public investigation names a counterparty.
head: Field checklist
speak: Odebrecht was one of Latin America's largest construction groups. Brazil's Operation Car Wash began in 2014, its chief executive was arrested in 2015, and in December 2016 the group and its affiliate Braskem entered a coordinated resolution with the United States, Brazil and Switzerland, admitting a dedicated division that managed bribe payments across many countries. The key decision was to institutionalise bribery: a budget, a staff and a parallel accounting system. The assumptions were that everyone paid, that offshore layers could not be traced, and that size meant protection. All failed. The point of no return was when bribery became a department, because revenue then depended on it. Liability reached the company through its agents and its books. Rule 72: never let anyone pay for a public decision on your behalf; every intermediary must show visible work, be paid into their own account at a defensible price, and be checked before engagement.
terms: Operation Car Wash (Lava Jato) — the Brazilian investigation, opened in 2014, that grew from money laundering into bribery around public contracts.
Intermediary — an agent, consultant or other third party who acts between a company and an official or customer, and through whom improper payments are often routed.
Books and records offence — in some regimes, a separate offence of falsely recording a payment, chargeable even apart from the bribe itself.

hostile.q: You paid a permitting consultant 150,000 dollars on a job where the permit was issued in three weeks. What did that money buy?
hostile.a: It bought a defined scope, and I can show it: the engagement letter, the drawings and submissions the consultant prepared, the meeting records with the authority, and the invoices tied to those deliverables. The fee was benchmarked against two other quotes. It was paid into the consultant's own account in this country. If any of that evidence is missing, I will tell you so and we will investigate before anything else is paid.

rule: Rule 72: Never let anyone pay for a public decision on your behalf; every agent, consultant and intermediary must show work you can see, be paid into their own account at a price you can defend, and be checked before engagement, not after.

title: What Integrity Costs, and What a Tainted Dollar Costs More
summary: Compliance has a visible cost in time and fees, but the hidden cost of a failure is larger: equity that cannot be drawn, accounts that are closed, and a buyer pool that shrinks at exit. Two worked examples put numbers on it. Warrick's Wealth Ledger and a note on ethics close the lesson.
body:
Integrity controls cost real money and slow a closing by days. A single investor who fails a check two weeks before closing can cost more than ten years of those controls, because equity that cannot be used must be replaced on worse terms, under time pressure.

Recall

Q. What is a beneficial owner?

A. The natural person who ultimately owns or controls an entity, found by tracing ownership and control through every layer of companies.

Q. Name one exemption concept used to raise capital without a full prospectus.

A. Many regimes exempt offerings to investors who meet defined wealth or sophistication tests, or to a limited number of people close to the issuer. The tests are jurisdictional; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. Why does recapture matter on an exit?

A. Depreciation claimed while owning a building can be added back as income when it is sold above its tax cost, so part of the gain may be taxed differently from capital. The rules are jurisdictional.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, lenders and investors read integrity as a credit question. A project whose equity cannot be explained is a project whose equity may disappear, and a lender sizes its risk to the worst plausible day. I want you to see the money in two places: the cost of doing it right, which is small and predictable, and the cost of a failure, which is large and arrives at the worst moment.

The visible cost: a budget line, not a mood

In plain English: KYC, screening and legal review are soft costs. Put them in the budget.

The professional framing: integrity costs fall into three buckets. Onboarding cost, the hours and fees to identify, verify and screen each counterparty. Monitoring cost, the re-screening of counterparties and buyers over the life of the project. And review cost, the legal advice on high-risk counterparties and on contract clauses. On a hypothetical 30,000,000 dollar project with 20 investors, 80 buyers and 30 consultants and contractors, you might budget a screening tool, a few days of a compliance consultant's time each quarter and a legal review of high-risk files. Whatever the figure, it is a small fraction of 1 percent of cost, and it is known in advance.

Worked example one: the investor who fails a check

Hypothetical round numbers. A project needs 6,000,000 dollars of equity. One investor has committed 1,500,000 dollars. Two weeks before the loan closes, the investor cannot explain the source of a 1,000,000 dollar transfer and will not identify a 40 percent owner of his holding company. You decline the money.

Now count the cost. The lender will not close until equity is fully committed, so the closing slips. Suppose it slips three months. The land loan, at a hypothetical 8 percent on 5,000,000 dollars, costs about 100,000 dollars of interest for those three months. The construction contract carries an escalation clause that adds a hypothetical 1 percent to a 20,000,000 dollar contract, or 200,000 dollars. And the replacement equity comes from a fund that demands a higher preferred return, worth, say, 300,000 dollars more over the life of the deal. Total: about 600,000 dollars. That is the cost of discovering the problem two weeks before closing. The same check run at the term sheet stage costs a phone call and a polite no.

Say that out loud now.

The check is cheap at the term sheet and expensive at the closing. I run it first.

Worked example two: what taking the money would have cost

Suppose instead the developer accepts the money. Eighteen months later the investor's funds are frozen by an authority, and the bank, applying its own policy, closes the project account. Three things follow. The lender's loan agreement almost certainly contains representations that no proceeds of crime are in the project and that no sanctioned person holds an interest; a breach is an event of default. The developer must move banking under default conditions. And at exit, every buyer's lawyer finds the history.

Price the exit. A hypothetical stabilised net operating income (NOI) of 1,800,000 dollars at a 6 percent capitalisation rate is worth 30,000,000 dollars. If the taint shrinks the buyer pool so that the best remaining bid prices at 6.5 percent, value falls to about 27,700,000 dollars, a loss of roughly 2,300,000 dollars, before counting legal costs or the time the asset spent unsellable. A reputation discount is invisible in a pro forma until the day it is the only number that matters.

How a lender reads your integrity file

When I sit on the lender's side, I do not ask whether you are honest. I ask whether your file would survive my own compliance team, because my bank will be judged on what it financed. Three things move my view of your credit. First, completeness: every investor, every beneficial owner and every major counterparty identified, with dates. Second, timing: checks run before money moved, not reconstructed afterwards. Third, ownership: one named person in your company who owns the file and can answer a question within a day.

A file like that does not lower your interest rate by a published amount; pricing is commercial practice and no lender will promise you a number for it. What it does is shorten approvals, reduce the conditions precedent I add to the term sheet, and make me far more willing to grant a waiver when something else goes wrong. That is worth more than a few basis points, because a waiver granted on time can save a project.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, integrity shows up as the reliability of every asset's title and every account's access. An asset with a clouded history is less liquid, so it belongs lower in your liquidity tiers whatever its appraised value. A banking relationship is itself an asset: years of clean files make the next account opening, the next credit line and the next cross-border transfer faster. Guard it as you would guard capital, because losing it means you cannot move capital at all.

Ethics and anti-corruption

The developers who stay clean over a long career rarely do it by heroic refusals. They do it by deciding in advance, in writing, what they will not do, so that the decision is not made under pressure in a hallway with a deal at stake. A rule written on a quiet day is far stronger than a resolution reached in a hard moment.

Write yours this week: three things you will never pay for, three counterparties you will never accept, and the one person you will call the moment a request feels wrong. Keep it short enough to remember.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is late discovery, when replacing tainted capital is most expensive and declining it is hardest. The control is to put every investor through KYC and source-of-funds checks before any commitment is counted in the capital plan.

The beginner's mistake

Leaving integrity costs out of the budget, then treating them as an annoyance to minimise. A line you budgeted is a line you will actually spend. The second mistake is measuring compliance by its cost alone, without ever pricing the failure it prevents; run both numbers side by side and the argument ends quickly.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman built stress tests with base, downside and severe cases. Add an integrity case to that set: one investor fails a check at closing, and one counterparty is named in an investigation mid-construction. Run both through the schedule and the exit value, and you will see why the check belongs at the front of the deal.

Recap

Integrity has a small, predictable cost and a failure has a large, late one: delayed closings, replacement equity on worse terms, default risk and an exit discount. Budget the controls, run them early, and treat your banking relationships as an asset.

Next: REGA on The Rules: the four legal regimes behind AML, beneficial ownership, anti-bribery and sanctions.
checklist: I budget onboarding, monitoring and legal review of counterparties as soft costs.
I count no investor commitment in the capital plan until KYC and source of funds clear.
I run checks at the term sheet stage, not at closing.
I add an integrity scenario to every stress test.
I read every loan representation about proceeds of crime and sanctions before signing.
I treat a clouded asset as less liquid on my personal balance sheet.
I have written down what I will never pay for and whom I will call.
head: Field checklist
speak: Integrity has two costs. The visible one is small: onboarding, monitoring and legal review, a known soft-cost line that is a fraction of 1 percent of cost. The hidden one is large. In a hypothetical case, an investor fails a source-of-funds check two weeks before closing; the closing slips three months, carrying cost, escalation and replacement equity on worse terms add up to about 600,000 dollars. Had the developer taken the money, a later freeze could close the bank account, breach loan representations and shrink the buyer pool at exit; a half-point move in the cap rate on a 30,000,000 dollar asset is a loss of about 2,300,000 dollars. So I budget the controls, I run every check before a commitment counts in the capital plan, and I treat my banking relationships as an asset in their own right, because without them I cannot move capital at all.
terms: Onboarding cost — the time and fees spent identifying, verifying and screening a counterparty before dealing with it.
Event of default — a defined failure in a loan agreement, such as a breached representation, that lets the lender stop funding and enforce.
Reputation discount — the reduction in price or financing terms caused by an asset's or sponsor's damaged history.

hostile.q: Your equity raise is short by 1,500,000 dollars two weeks before closing. Why should I not just assume you will find it?
hostile.a: Because I am not asking you to assume. I declined that commitment because the investor could not document his source of funds, and I would rather be short than wrong. Here is the replacement plan: two named sources, their commitment dates, the cost difference on the preferred return and the revised closing date. I have also run the delay through the carrying cost and the escalation clause so you can see the full number.

title: The Four Regimes: Money Laundering, Ownership, Bribery and Sanctions
summary: Four separate bodies of law govern integrity in a development business: anti-money-laundering rules, beneficial ownership transparency, anti-bribery statutes and sanctions. Each has a different trigger and a different standard of fault. This lesson maps them so you know which question to ask your lawyer.
body:
Integrity law is not one rule but four regimes, and they fail you in different ways. Money-laundering law punishes what you should have noticed, bribery law reaches what your agents did, ownership law demands what you must disclose, and sanctions law forbids what you must not touch, almost regardless of intent.

Recall

Q. Why does a late failed investor check cost more than an early one?

A. Because the closing slips, carrying cost and escalation run, and replacement equity is raised under time pressure on worse terms.

Q. What is fiduciary duty, in concept, in an investment vehicle?

A. A duty, where it applies, to act in the investors' interest rather than your own: loyalty, care and honest disclosure of conflicts. Whether it applies depends on the structure and the governing law.

Q. In an exit, what does a buyer inherit in a share sale that it does not in an asset sale?

A. The company's history: its tax attributes and its liabilities, including any unresolved compliance problems.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will not draft these rules and you should not try to interpret them alone. What you need is a map: which regime a situation falls under, what triggers it and how strict it is. Then you can brief a lawyer in two minutes and recognise when an ordinary business request has crossed a line. Every specific in this lesson is a concept, not a jurisdictional conclusion. Verify any rule, threshold or deadline against the primary source before you rely on it.

Regime one: anti-money laundering

In plain English: laws that make certain businesses check their customers, keep records and report suspicion.

The professional framing: an anti-money-laundering (AML) regime designates reporting entities, typically banks, lawyers handling client money, real estate brokers and, in some places, developers [unverified — confirm independently]. Their core duties are customer identification, risk assessment, record-keeping for a set period, and reporting suspicious transactions to a national financial intelligence unit. Two features catch people out. The standard of fault is often not knowledge but reasonable grounds to suspect, so ignoring an obvious red flag is not a defence. And many regimes forbid tipping off: telling the customer that a report has been made or is being considered.

A worked example, hypothetical. A buyer offers to pay the full 500,000 dollar price of a unit in cash instruments from several sources, and asks that the sale price on the agreement be stated lower. Even if you are not a reporting entity, your broker and your lawyer may be, and the request itself is a set of red flags: structured funds, multiple sources and a request to falsify a document. You do not accept the arrangement, you do not discuss reporting with the buyer, and you tell your lawyer the same day.

Regime two: beneficial ownership transparency

In plain English: laws that require companies to know, record and sometimes publish who really owns them.

Many jurisdictions now require companies to keep a register of individuals with significant control, and some require filing it with a public or government registry. Some property registries also ask who stands behind a corporate buyer. The thresholds, the definition of control and who may see the register differ; verify against the primary source. For you this runs in both directions. Your counterparties' registers help your KYC. Your own companies need accurate registers, kept current whenever shares move, because a lender, a buyer and a regulator will all ask.

Say that out loud now.

Money laundering punishes what I should have noticed. Bribery reaches what my agents did. Ownership law makes me disclose. Sanctions forbid me to touch.

Regime three: anti-bribery

In plain English: laws that make it a crime to give or receive anything of value to improperly influence a decision.

The professional framing: modern anti-bribery statutes typically cover public officials, often private-sector bribery too, and foreign officials when your country's law reaches abroad. Well-known examples include the United States Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the United Kingdom Bribery Act 2010 and Canada's Corruption of Foreign Public Officials Act. Common features, in concept: liability for payments made through intermediaries; corporate liability for acts of employees and agents; and in some regimes an offence of failing to prevent bribery, with a defence for companies that had adequate procedures in place. That last feature turns your written policies, training and third-party checks into legal evidence.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A local consultant proposes a 2 percent success fee on a 20,000,000 dollar contract award, 400,000 dollars, for introducing you to the decision maker. A success fee tied to an official's decision, paid to someone whose work is access, is a classic structure for a bribe. The lawful version, if one exists, is a fee for defined, visible work at a market rate, with anti-corruption representations, audit rights and a termination right in the contract.

Regime four: sanctions

In plain English: legal lists of people, entities and countries you must not deal with.

Sanctions are issued by governments and international bodies and can freeze assets, prohibit transactions and restrict whole sectors. Two features matter most. They are close to strict liability in many regimes, so good faith does not excuse a prohibited deal. And many lists extend to entities owned or controlled by a listed person even when the entity itself is not named, so screening the company is not enough; screen its owners. The consequence for a developer is practical: screen before signing, screen before paying, and screen again when a list changes.

Where they meet: politically exposed persons

A politically exposed person, often shortened to PEP, is someone who holds or recently held a prominent public function, along with close family and associates. Being a PEP is not wrongdoing. It raises risk because the person is in a position to be offered bribes or to misuse public funds, so AML rules usually call for enhanced checks on source of wealth and senior approval before dealing. A PEP who wants to invest in your project triggers all four regimes at once, which is exactly when to slow down.

How the regimes show up in your contracts

You meet these laws most often as clauses, not statutes. A loan agreement will carry representations that the borrower and its owners are not sanctioned, that no proceeds of crime are in the project and that no bribe has been paid, plus a covenant to keep those statements true and to notify the lender if they stop being true. A joint venture agreement should carry the same representations from your partner, a right to audit, a right to exit or buy out a partner who breaches them, and a duty to cooperate with KYC requests. A consultant's or agent's engagement letter should carry anti-corruption undertakings, a ban on sub-agents without consent and a termination right without compensation on breach.

Read each of these as a promise about facts you must be able to prove. If you cannot produce the evidence behind a representation on the day you sign it, you are not ready to sign. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer qualified in each governing law.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating these regimes as one generic compliance box, and so applying the bribery mindset, where intent matters, to sanctions, where it often does not. The control is a written map, reviewed by your lawyer, that says which regime covers each type of counterparty and what check it triggers.

The beginner's mistake

Asking only whether something is legal here. Anti-bribery and sanctions laws can follow a payment through the currency, the bank or the nationality of the people involved. Ask which countries' laws could reach the transaction.

Callback

In Week 63, REGA and Omar covered foreign investment registration, capital controls and banking relationships. The four regimes today are the reason a bank asks you what it asks: the bank is itself a reporting entity, screening for sanctions and judged on its AML controls. When you understand its rules, its questions stop feeling personal.

Recap

Four regimes: AML, with reasonable-suspicion fault and no tipping off; beneficial ownership, demanding accurate registers; anti-bribery, reaching agents and rewarding adequate procedures; and sanctions, near-strict and extending to owned entities. PEPs trigger all four.

Next: Cole on The Numbers: reverse engineering a frozen account back to the hidden owner and the unexplained dollar.
checklist: I can name which of the four regimes applies to each type of counterparty.
I never tell a counterparty that a suspicion report is being considered.
I keep my own companies' ownership registers current every time shares move.
I refuse success fees tied to an official's decision.
I screen owners as well as entities against sanctions lists.
I require senior approval and enhanced source-of-wealth checks for any politically exposed person.
I ask which countries' laws could reach a transaction, not only the local one.
head: Field checklist
speak: Integrity law is four regimes. Anti-money-laundering rules make reporting entities identify customers, keep records and report suspicion, often on a standard of reasonable grounds to suspect, and they forbid tipping off. Beneficial ownership rules require companies to know and record the real people behind them, so my own registers must be current. Anti-bribery statutes reach payments through agents, make companies liable for their people, and in some regimes create an offence of failing to prevent bribery, with a defence for adequate procedures, which turns my policies into evidence. Sanctions forbid dealing with listed people and often their owned entities, close to strict liability, so I screen owners before signing and before paying. A politically exposed person triggers all four, which is exactly when to slow down and get senior approval. Every specific is jurisdictional, so I verify with counsel before relying on it.
terms: Tipping off — telling a customer, directly or indirectly, that a suspicious transaction report has been made or is being considered, which many AML regimes forbid.
Politically exposed person (PEP) — someone who holds or recently held a prominent public function, or a close family member or associate, who calls for enhanced checks.
Adequate procedures — a company's documented anti-bribery policies, training and controls, which in some regimes form a defence to a failure-to-prevent offence.

hostile.q: Your joint venture partner's holding company is not on any sanctions list. Why are you still not satisfied?
hostile.a: Because many sanctions regimes reach entities that are owned or controlled by a listed person even when the entity is not named. Screening the company is only half the check. I need its ownership chain to the natural persons, each of them screened, and confirmation of who controls it by other means, such as board appointment rights. Until that is done, we do not sign and we do not move money.

title: Reverse Engineering a Frozen Account
summary: Week 72 is an even week, so we start from a finished outcome and work backward: a bank has frozen a project account, and we trace the decision back to a hidden owner and an unexplained dollar. Two worked calculations, an ownership chain and a source-of-funds reconciliation, use hypothetical round numbers.
body:
When a bank freezes an account, it has already done arithmetic you did not do. Reverse engineering its decision teaches you to run that arithmetic yourself, before the money arrives, with two tools: effective ownership multiplied down a chain, and a source-of-funds reconciliation that must close to the dollar.

Recall

Q. In anti-money-laundering law, what is tipping off?

A. Telling a customer that a suspicious transaction report has been made or is being considered, which many regimes forbid.

Q. What does a sponsor's investor report have to avoid, in concept?

A. Misleading statements and material omissions: it must report results and material events honestly against what the offering documents promised.

Q. What is a step-up in tax cost, in concept, on an exit or departure?

A. An adjustment that resets an asset's tax cost, often to market value, so later gains are measured from the new figure. Whether and when it applies is jurisdictional; verify against the primary source.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will rarely be told exactly why a bank acted. Banks are often not permitted to explain, because the same tipping-off rules that bind you bind them. What you can do is reconstruct the likely reasons from the facts in your own file, and then build your files so that the same arithmetic comes out clean next time.

Do not ask the bank to confirm a theory, and do not tell the investor what you suspect. Your job in the first hour is to stop accepting new money from that source, preserve every document, and call your lawyer. Your job in the following week is the arithmetic below. Every number in it is hypothetical.

The finished outcome

A project company's account is frozen three days after it receives a 2,000,000 dollar equity wire from Investor Holdings Ltd. The bank's letter says only that it is reviewing the account under its legal obligations. Work backward. There are two likely questions behind that letter: who really owns Investor Holdings, and where did the 2,000,000 dollars come from. We test each.

Worked calculation one: effective ownership

Step 1. Write the chain as the documents show it. Investor Holdings Ltd is owned 50 percent by Alpha Corp and 50 percent by Beta Corp. Alpha Corp is owned 60 percent by Ms A and 40 percent by Mr B. Beta Corp is owned 70 percent by Gamma Trust Company, as nominee, and 30 percent by Mr B.

Step 2. Multiply down each path. Ms A: 50 percent of 60 percent, which is 30 percent. Mr B through Alpha: 50 percent of 40 percent, 20 percent. Mr B through Beta: 50 percent of 30 percent, 15 percent. Gamma's nominee holding: 50 percent of 70 percent, 35 percent.

Step 3. Add each person's paths together. Mr B holds 20 plus 15, which is 35 percent. That is the step beginners miss: no single holding crossed the threshold, but the sum did.

Step 4. Look through the nominee. A nominee holds shares for someone else. The 35 percent held by Gamma belongs to an unnamed principal. Until that person is identified, more than a third of the investor is unknown.

Step 5. Check control as well as ownership. Suppose Alpha Corp's articles give Mr B the right to appoint the board. Then Mr B controls the holding company regardless of his percentage.

Result: three beneficial owners need identifying, Ms A at 30 percent, Mr B at 35 percent with control rights, and the hidden principal behind the 35 percent nominee holding. On a 25 percent test, used here as a hypothetical figure, all three qualify. The file the developer held named only Ms A, because she signed the subscription agreement.

Say that out loud now.

Multiply down every path, add each person's paths together, look through every nominee, then check control.

Worked calculation two: the reconciliation that would not close

Now the money. The investor's explanation was that the 2,000,000 dollars came from Alpha Corp's sale of a warehouse. Reconcile it backward from the wire to the sale.

Step 1. Start with the sale. The sale statement shows a price of 5,000,000 dollars.

Step 2. Subtract what left before the money was free: a mortgage discharge of 2,400,000 dollars, transaction costs of 150,000 dollars and an estimated tax reserve of 450,000 dollars. That leaves 2,000,000 dollars of net proceeds.

Step 3. Follow the account. Alpha Corp's bank statement shows the 2,000,000 dollars arriving and, a week later, 1,000,000 dollars leaving to Investor Holdings. That is only half.

Step 4. Find the rest. Investor Holdings' statement shows a second 1,000,000 dollars arriving the same week from an account in a third country, held by a company not in the ownership chain at all.

Step 5. State the gap. 2,000,000 dollars wired to the project; 1,000,000 dollars traced to the warehouse; 1,000,000 dollars with no documented source.

Each calculation alone might have been explained. Together they are what a bank's analyst sees: an unidentified owner of over a third of the investor, and half the money arriving from outside the story. That is a frozen account.

Worked calculation three: the fee that is out of proportion

The same reverse method exposes a bribe hidden as a fee. The finished outcome is an invoice: a permitting consultant bills 150,000 dollars on a project whose permit was issued in a month. Work backward to the implied price of the work.

Step 1. List the deliverables the consultant can show: two application packages, four meetings with the authority and a set of responses to comments.

Step 2. Estimate the hours honestly, using your own experience or a second quote: say 10 working days.

Step 3. Divide. 150,000 dollars across 10 days is 15,000 dollars a day.

Step 4. Compare with the market. If comparable consultants charge a hypothetical 1,500 dollars a day, the invoice is ten times the market price for the visible work.

Step 5. Name the unexplained amount. At market rates the visible work is worth about 15,000 dollars, which leaves about 135,000 dollars that buys something you cannot see. That is not proof of a bribe. It is a number you must explain before you pay, and a reason to call your lawyer if you cannot.

Run it forward next time

Reverse engineering is only useful if it changes the front end. The forward version is a one-page intake for every equity investor: the full chain to natural persons with each path multiplied and summed, nominees looked through, control rights listed, and a source-of-funds reconciliation that closes to the dollar from the originating event to the wire into your account. A wire that does not match the reconciliation is returned to its sender, not held while you ask.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting the person who signs as the person who owns. Signatories are often employees, lawyers or nominees. The control is to require the full chain before the subscription is accepted, and to refuse any holding whose principal will not be named.

The beginner's mistake

Checking each holding against the threshold separately and never adding one person's indirect paths together. Ownership through two companies is still ownership.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage reverse engineered a deal from public information: the implied land price, rent and return. The method is the same here. Take the outcome you can see, list the inputs that must have produced it, and test each until the arithmetic closes. Whether the outcome is a sale price or a frozen account, the discipline is to make the numbers reconcile.

Recap

From a frozen account we worked back to two failures: a hidden 35 percent owner found by summing indirect paths and looking through a nominee, and 1,000,000 dollars with no documented source. The forward control is an intake that multiplies, sums, looks through and reconciles before any wire is accepted.

Next: REGA on The Room: the investor who does not want to complete your KYC form.
checklist: I write every ownership chain down to natural persons.
I multiply each path and add each person's paths together.
I look through every nominee and trust company to the principal.
I list control rights, such as board appointment, separately from percentages.
I reconcile source of funds from the originating event to the wire, to the dollar.
I return any wire that does not match the reconciliation.
I never treat the signatory as the owner without evidence.
head: Field checklist
speak: Start from the outcome: a bank freezes a project account after a 2,000,000 dollar equity wire. Work backward. First, ownership. Multiply down every path and add each person's paths together. Mr B held 20 percent through one company and 15 through another, 35 percent in total, though no single holding crossed the threshold. A nominee held another 35 percent for an unnamed principal, and Mr B had board appointment rights, which is control. Second, money. The investor said it came from a warehouse sale. The sale price of 5,000,000 dollars, less mortgage, costs and a tax reserve, left 2,000,000 dollars, but only 1,000,000 reached the investor from that sale. The other 1,000,000 arrived from a company outside the chain. Hidden owner plus unexplained money equals a frozen account. Next time I run it forward: full chain, paths summed, nominees looked through, a reconciliation that closes to the dollar before any wire is accepted.
terms: Effective ownership — the share of an entity a person holds once every indirect path through intermediate companies is multiplied out and added together.
Nominee — a person or company holding shares or assets in its own name on behalf of someone else, the principal.
Reconciliation — a step-by-step tie of one figure to another, here from the originating event to the wire received, that must close exactly.

hostile.q: Your investor's file names one shareholder. Our analysis says three people own or control it. Which of us is right?
hostile.a: You are, and I can show you how I would have got there: each path multiplied and summed, the nominee holding looked through, and the board appointment right treated as control. I will not draw the funds until all three people are identified and verified and the source-of-funds reconciliation closes. If it does not close, the wire goes back to its sender.

title: The Investor Who Will Not Fill In the Form
summary: A respected introducer brings an investor ready to commit a large cheque, on one condition: no ownership disclosure beyond a signatory. This scene gives you the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent and how to hold your state when the money is on the table.
body:
The hardest integrity conversation is not with a criminal. It is with a polite, wealthy, well-introduced person who is offended by your questions, while your raise is short and the closing is close. You hold the line by making the check impersonal, the same for everyone, and by being willing to lose the money.

Recall

Q. When you trace effective ownership, what must you do after multiplying each path?

A. Add each person's paths together, look through nominees to the principal, and check control rights separately from percentages.

Q. In a securities offering, why is marketing restricted under many exemptions?

A. Because the exemption assumes a limited or qualified group of investors; general solicitation can take an offering outside it. The rules are jurisdictional; verify against the primary source.

Q. Why might a buyer prefer an asset sale to a share sale?

A. Because it takes the building without the seller company's history of liabilities and tax positions, though it may cost more in transfer tax.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the scene below is hypothetical, but its shape is common. Your capital plan is 1,500,000 dollars short with five weeks to closing. A senior figure you respect introduces a family investor ready to commit 2,000,000 dollars through a holding company. The subscription agreement arrives signed by a director. The KYC form comes back with the beneficial owner section blank and a note: our principal values privacy; our introducer can vouch for us. You are meeting the director and the introducer at the investor's office.

The question behind the question

When the director says, do you not trust us, the real question is whether you will bend. A person with nothing to hide usually completes a confidential KYC form once it is explained, because they deal with banks every week and know the drill. A person who resists strongly is telling you something about the cost of disclosure to them. Your task is not to accuse. It is to find out which of the two you are facing, and to make the decision depend on documents rather than on the relationship.

The lines to say

  • Thank you for the confidence. Our process is the same for every investor, including my own companies, and it is what our lender and our bank require of us.
  • Here is exactly what we need and who will see it: the ownership chain to the natural persons, identity documents for each person above the threshold, and a source-of-funds note for this commitment. It stays in a confidential file, seen by me, our compliance adviser and, if asked, our lender.
  • If privacy is the concern, we can sign a confidentiality agreement covering the file. What we cannot do is accept funds without it.
  • If the principal prefers not to proceed on that basis, I understand, and I will be grateful for the introduction.

Say that out loud now.

Our process is the same for every investor, and without it we cannot accept the funds.

The lines never to say

  • We can sort the paperwork out after closing. You have just promised to accept money you have not checked.
  • Just give me something for the file. That invites a document created to satisfy you rather than to tell the truth.
  • I am sure it is fine, but the bank is very strict. Blaming the bank tells them you would skip the check if you could.
  • Are you laundering money? Never accuse. If you have a suspicion, you take it to your lawyer, not to the counterparty, and in many regimes you must not tip them off.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after you state the requirement. The director will fill the silence with reasons, offers to vouch, perhaps a hint that another project would welcome the money. Let it come. Each sentence is information. Stay silent, too, after the introducer offers his word. His reputation is real and worth recording, but it is not a document, and saying nothing for a moment makes that clear without insulting him.

A worked example of the trade

Before the meeting, write the arithmetic on one card so you are not negotiating against your own fear. Hypothetical: if you decline, the closing slips about two months while you raise replacement equity, costing roughly 70,000 dollars of land-loan interest and a 150,000 dollar escalation on the contract, about 220,000 dollars in all. If you accept and the funds are later frozen, you face a closed account, a possible event of default under your loan and a damaged exit. You already know which number is larger. The card means you do not have to work it out under pressure.

A second example. The director offers a middle path: the principal will disclose to your lawyer only, not to you. That can be acceptable, if your lawyer is the one running the KYC, confirms in writing that every owner above the threshold is identified, verified and screened, and the file is available to your lender on request. Whether it is acceptable depends on the regime and the lender; ask your lawyer before you agree.

How to hold your state

Your body will read this meeting as a threat to the deal. Before you go in, while you are parked, take two slow breaths with a longer exhale; it is a simple practitioner habit for lowering arousal, and if you have any concern about breathing drills, check that with your doctor. Put the card in your pocket. In the room, speak more slowly than feels natural, keep your hands still and keep your tone warm. Warmth and firmness are not opposites. The person who stays friendly while refusing to move is the one who controls the room.

How it can end, and what you do next

The meeting has three likely endings, and you should know your next step for each before you walk in.

First, they agree. Thank them, send the confidentiality agreement and the KYC list the same afternoon, and give a date by which the file must be complete for the commitment to count. Do not count the money in your capital plan until it is.

Second, they take the lawyer-only route. Confirm the arrangement in writing with your own lawyer, not theirs, and get your lender's agreement that it satisfies the loan's requirements before you rely on it.

Third, they refuse, or they go quiet. Close politely in writing: we have not been able to complete our onboarding and so cannot accept the commitment. Keep a dated note of what was asked, what was offered and what you decided. If anything in the meeting gave you grounds to suspect the money, take that note to your lawyer, who can advise whether you or anyone advising you has a reporting duty. Then start the replacement raise that afternoon, not after a week of hoping they will come back.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the relationship with the introducer makes the decision for you. The control is to decide the rule before the meeting, in writing, and to bring someone, your compliance adviser or your lawyer, who can say the requirement in a neutral voice.

The beginner's mistake

Apologising for the process. An apology tells the other side the rule is negotiable. Explain it once, clearly, and then let it stand.

Callback

In Week 66, Kema and JAX taught BATNA, your best alternative to a negotiated agreement. Your BATNA here is replacement equity at a known cost. When you have priced it, you are not choosing between this investor and failure; you are choosing between this investor and a slightly worse deal. That is what lets you stay calm.

Recap

State the same requirement you apply to everyone, explain what is needed and who sees it, offer confidentiality, never accept money unchecked and never accuse. Price the alternative before you go in, stay silent after the requirement, and be willing to lose the cheque.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap, with Cole in the Auditor's Chair.
checklist: I decide the KYC rule in writing before any investor meeting.
I explain exactly what is needed and who will see it.
I offer a confidentiality agreement rather than an exception.
I never accept funds before the file is complete.
I never accuse a counterparty or hint at a report.
I price my alternative before the meeting and carry it on one card.
I record an introducer's reputation but never rely on it in place of documents.
head: Field checklist
speak: A respected introducer brings an investor with a 2,000,000 dollar cheque and a blank beneficial owner section. The real question behind 'do you not trust us' is whether I will bend. I answer with the same rule I apply to everyone: the ownership chain to natural persons, identity documents above the threshold, and a source-of-funds note, kept in a confidential file seen only by me, our compliance adviser and, if asked, our lender. I offer a confidentiality agreement, not an exception. I never say we will sort it out after closing, never ask for something just for the file, never blame the bank and never accuse. I stay silent after stating the requirement and let them fill the silence. Before the meeting I price my alternative, replacement equity at about 220,000 dollars of delay cost, so I am choosing between this investor and a slightly worse deal, not between this investor and failure.
terms: Introducer — a person who connects a developer with an investor or counterparty, whose recommendation is information but not evidence.
Confidentiality agreement — a contract limiting who may see and use shared information, here offered to protect an investor's KYC file.
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA) — what you will do if this deal does not happen, which sets how firmly you can hold a position.

hostile.q: Our principal has invested with three other developers who never asked for any of this. Why are you different?
hostile.a: I cannot speak for them. I can tell you what we owe our lender and our bank, and that we apply it to every investor, including my own companies. We are happy to protect the file with a confidentiality agreement, or to let our lawyer hold it. If that does not work for your principal, I understand, and I would still be grateful for the conversation.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 72 Review: Integrity as a Control System
summary: Six questions test the week: the four integrity controls, beneficial ownership, source of funds, bribery through agents, sanctions and the reluctant investor. Week 72 is a fourth week, so Cole takes the Auditor's Chair to read a hypothetical investor onboarding memo as a hostile auditor would. A two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: integrity is something you can prove from a file, and every investor, agent and buyer goes into the same file before any money moves.

Recall

Q. What is a nominee shareholder?

A. A person or company holding shares in its own name on behalf of an unnamed principal, who must be looked through to find the beneficial owner.

Q. In an offering, what does a misrepresentation claim usually turn on?

A. Whether an untrue statement or misleading omission was about something a reasonable investor would treat as important.

Q. What is the core tax difference between selling a building and selling the company that owns it?

A. In an asset sale the company sells the building and is taxed on its gain; in a share sale the owner sells the company and the building's tax history passes to the buyer.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the integrity file is one of the few documents every future lender, buyer and regulator will read. If you can answer these six questions aloud, without notes, you can sit with a bank's compliance officer as an equal. Answer each before reading the answer.

Notice that most answers are procedures rather than definitions. That is deliberate. In this subject, knowing what a beneficial owner is matters far less than knowing the five steps you take to find one, and being able to show a lender that you took them, in order, before any money moved.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the four integrity controls a developer runs?

Answer: Know the counterparty and its beneficial owners; trace source of funds and test source of wealth; never pay for a public decision directly or through anyone; and screen every party against sanctions lists before signing and paying.

Question 2. How do you find a beneficial owner in a layered chain?

Answer: Multiply down each path, add each person's paths together, look through nominees to the principal, and check control rights such as board appointment separately from percentages.

Question 3. What is the difference between source of funds and source of wealth?

Answer: Source of funds is the documented trail of the specific money in this transaction. Source of wealth is how the person built their overall wealth, tested for plausibility against the commitment.

Question 4. Why is a payment through an agent still your risk?

Answer: Because modern anti-bribery laws commonly reach payments made through intermediaries and make companies liable for what their agents do on their behalf; some also create an offence of failing to prevent bribery.

Question 5. Why is screening the company not enough for sanctions?

Answer: Because many regimes extend prohibitions to entities owned or controlled by a listed person even when the entity is not named, so the owners must be screened too.

Question 6. What do you do when an investor will not complete KYC?

Answer: Apply the same rule as for everyone, offer confidentiality rather than an exception, never accept the funds unchecked, never accuse or tip off, record what happened, and start the replacement raise.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

REGA framed integrity as four controls. Ford and Cole took Odebrecht, where bribery became a department, giving Rule 72. Roman priced the cost of a late failed check and of a tainted exit. REGA mapped the four legal regimes and the politically exposed person. Cole reverse engineered a frozen account back to a hidden owner and an unexplained million. REGA ran the meeting with the investor who would not fill in the form.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 72 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair. Read this hypothetical onboarding memo as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Onboarding memo: Investor Holdings Ltd, commitment 2,000,000 dollars. Beneficial owner: Ms A, director and signatory, verified by passport. Other shareholders hold under 25 percent each and need no review. Source of funds: sale of a warehouse; sale statement on file. Sanctions screen: Investor Holdings Ltd screened, no match, dated at the term sheet four months ago. Introduced by a long-standing business contact who vouches for the principal. Recommendation: accept; complete any outstanding items after closing. Prepared by: Project Coordinator.

The defects. First, the memo treats the signatory as the beneficial owner; a director who signs is not necessarily an owner, and the chain was never written down. Second, it tests each holding separately against the threshold; indirect paths were never added together, and nominees were never looked through. Third, the source of funds stops at the sale statement and never reconciles the sale proceeds to the wire, so a gap of any size would be invisible. Fourth, the sanctions screen covers the company only, not its owners, and is four months stale. Fifth, the introducer's word is recorded as if it were evidence. Sixth, the recommendation to complete items after closing defeats the purpose of onboarding. Seventh, it is prepared by a coordinator with no stated approval by the person accountable for the integrity file.

Then the auditor asks for the evidence that should sit behind each line: the full ownership chart with paths multiplied and summed; identity documents for each person above the threshold; the nominee's declaration naming its principal; a reconciliation from the sale to the wire; a fresh screen of the company and every owner; and the name and signature of the approver. A memo that cannot produce those in an hour is a memo written to close the deal, not to protect it.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a new partner who asks, why do we make investors jump through hoops? Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because the money in our project has to be explainable to our lender, our bank and every future buyer. We run four checks. We identify every investor and the real people behind any chain of companies, adding each person's indirect holdings together and looking through nominees. We trace the source of the specific money to the wire, to the dollar. We never pay anything for a public decision, and we hold every agent to visible work, a market price and an account in their own name. And we screen every party and its owners against sanctions lists before signing and paying. The checks cost a small, known amount. Skipping one can cost a delayed closing, a frozen account or a discounted exit. So nobody's money counts in our capital plan until the file is complete, and the rule is the same for everyone, including us."

Score your answer. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name all four controls? Did you say why the check comes before the money? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is pressure: a short capital plan, a close deadline and a respected introducer combine to make an exception feel reasonable. The control is a rule written in advance, applied to everyone, with a named owner who signs every file.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking integrity is about avoiding bad people. It is about being able to prove, from documents, that you checked. A good person with an incomplete file still costs you a frozen account.

Callback

In Week 56, Elias and Ford taught the substance record: evidence, kept as you go, of where decisions are really made. The integrity file is its twin. Both are worthless if reconstructed after a problem, and both are among your strongest defences if kept contemporaneously.

Recap

Four controls, four regimes, one file. Multiply and sum ownership, reconcile money to the dollar, hold agents to visible work, screen owners, and never let the closing date write the exception. Rule 72 keeps every public decision unbought.

checklist: What are the four integrity controls a developer runs?
How do you find a beneficial owner in a layered chain?
What is the difference between source of funds and source of wealth?
Why is a payment through an agent still your risk?
Why is screening the company not enough for sanctions?
What do you do when an investor will not complete KYC?
head: The six questions
speak: Integrity is something I can prove from a file. Four controls run before any money moves. I identify every investor and the real people behind any chain of companies, multiplying each path, adding each person's paths together and looking through nominees. I trace the source of the specific money to the wire, to the dollar. I never pay for a public decision, and every agent shows visible work, a market price and an account in their own name. And I screen every party and its owners against sanctions lists before signing and before paying. Four legal regimes sit behind those controls: anti-money laundering, beneficial ownership, anti-bribery and sanctions. When an investor will not complete the file, I apply the same rule as for everyone, offer confidentiality, never accuse and never accept the funds. Rule 72: never let anyone pay for a public decision on my behalf.
terms: Integrity file — the documented record of identity, ownership, source-of-funds and screening checks for every counterparty.
Stale screen — a sanctions or adverse-media search too old to rely on, because lists and facts change.
Contemporaneous record — evidence created at the time of the event, which carries far more weight than a later reconstruction.

hostile.q: Your onboarding memo says the remaining items will be completed after closing. Did your company accept money it had not checked?
hostile.a: On that memo, yes, and that is not acceptable. We will treat the commitment as not received, hold or return the funds on our lawyer's advice, complete the ownership chain, the reconciliation and a fresh screen of every owner, and have the accountable person approve the file. I will also change our process so that no commitment can be counted in the capital plan until the file is signed off.
